applicability.rationale: Patients were centrally randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to two parallel antiplatelet regimens.

approved_result.relation_rationale: The main report defines the primary composite as cardiovascular death, MI, definite stent thrombosis, ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, or TIMI major or minor bleeding; it reports this comparison at 12 months (335–394 days, censored at day 366) from randomization in the 1-month versus 12-month DAPT groups. The randomized assignment population is analyzed after excluding consent withdrawals, as specified by the authors.

reported.analysis_population: Intention-to-treat population after excluding patients who withdrew consent during follow-up: 1500 in the 1-month DAPT group and 1509 in the 12-month DAPT group; missing outcome data were censored at loss to follow-up.

endpoint.definition: Composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, definite stent thrombosis, ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, or TIMI major or minor bleeding
endpoint.name: Primary end point

approved_result.requested_outcome: Composite of cardiovascular death, MI, ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, definite stent thrombosis, or TIMI major or minor bleeding

target.intended_analysis_population: All randomized participants in the comparison groups

populations, which were defined as patients continuing the
randomized antiplatelet regimen on day 60 excluding and
including, respectively, those with protocol violations for
inclusion criteria. In addition, we performed a sensitivity
analysis assuming that patients lost to follow-up in the
1-month DAPT group had a primary end point event, while
those in the 12-month DAPT group did not have an event.

answers.justification: The flow shows 3045 randomized and 2974 with completed 1-year follow-up: 71 participants (2.3%) had no completed follow-up, including 45/1523 in the 1-month arm and 26/1522 in the 12-month arm (consent withdrawals plus loss to follow-up). Because the outcome is rare, 71 unavailable outcomes are not automatically negligible. In the sensitivity analysis for the 35 lost to follow-up, assigning events to all missing 1-month participants and none to 12-month participants changed the HR from 0.64 to 1.00; this could materially change the estimate. The sensitivity analysis does not clearly address the 36 consent withdrawals.
unknowns: The report does not establish whether outcome events were nevertheless ascertained for any participants who withdrew consent.
The sensitivity analysis addresses loss to follow-up but not clearly consent withdrawals.

answers.justification: A sensitivity analysis assigned every lost-to-follow-up participant in the experimental arm the event and none in control. Although noninferiority remained, the HR moved to 1.00 (95% CI 0.69–1.46) from 0.64, so the effect estimate was not little changed. This extreme scenario covers lost follow-up but not the consent withdrawals, and therefore does not establish that the reported result was free from missing-data bias.
unknowns: Whether the extreme sensitivity assumption spans plausible outcomes for the consent withdrawals.

answers.justification: The missingness reasons were not reported, so there is no direct evidence linking a particular participant's loss to an event. However, the missing participants withdrew or were lost during follow-up for a composite of serious cardiovascular and bleeding outcomes; their health status could plausibly be related to whether those outcomes occurred. The 1-month arm also had more missing follow-up than control. This supports possible outcome-dependent missingness, while the exact mechanism remains unknown.
unknowns: Reasons for loss to follow-up and consent withdrawal, and whether outcome data were available after withdrawal.
